meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users differed significantly from control groups at baseline (e.g., higher education 26.07% vs 11.94% in metformin; higher BMI ≥30 kg/m² 13.21% vs 4.87% in metformin and 3.04% in insulin). Key clinical confounders such as diabetes duration, baseline eGFR, microvascular complications, and glycemic control were unmeasured or had massive missingness (HbA1c missing in 90.52% of GLP-1 RA, 91.79% of insulin, and 90.45% of metformin users; Table 3S), confounding by indication/severity away from the null.

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Massive attrition during cohort definition (362,035 out of 742,437 eligible excluded solely for missing prescription data; 177,381 excluded for missing ID) and restriction to strict near-monotherapy (<6 months of other medications) selectively samples a non-representative subgroup.

findings.title: Heavy exclusion based on missing record parameters
findings.mechanism: Excluding 362,035 outpatients (36.7% of initial 985,278) for missing prescription data introduces selection bias if missingness relates to clinical adherence or outcome tracking.
evidence: 985,278 outpatients screened; 177,381 excluded for missing IDs, 362,035 excluded for missing prescription data, leaving 380,370 eligible (Figure 1)

findings.title: Conditioning on post-baseline medication continuation
findings.mechanism: Defining cohorts by cumulative prescription patterns lasting until end of follow-up introduces survivor/selection bias.
evidence: Patients required to have accumulative prescription lasting from baseline to last follow-up date with other drugs <6 months

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Treating acute drug-induced side effects (e.g. nausea/diarrhea) as competing events in Fine-Gray models differentially censors or alters risk sets for patients experiencing early toxicity versus chronic outcomes.

findings.title: Inappropriate competing risks specification
findings.mechanism: Common non-fatal side effects leading to discontinuation (dizziness, acne, diarrhea) were operationalized as competing risks rather than standard censoring or time-varying exposure transitions, distorting subdistribution hazard ratios.
evidence: Competing events were systematically defined as 'activated by any incidence of specific acute symptoms, including diarrhea/emesis, dermatitis tetter, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia, etc.'

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: Over 90% of HbA1c data (90.52% in GLP-1 RA, 91.79% in insulin, 90.45% in metformin) and ~33% of FPG data were missing at baseline. Instead of multiple imputation or complete case sensitivity analysis, missing values were treated as an informative 'unspecified' matching category, obscuring substantial baseline disease disparities.

findings.title: Extreme missingness in core metabolic markers
findings.mechanism: HbA1c and FPG are critical determinants of microvascular and macrovascular complications. Missingness above 90% invalidates baseline comparability despite apparent PSM balance.
evidence: HbA1c missing rate: 90.52% (GLP-1 RA), 91.79% (insulin), 90.45% (metformin) (Table 3S footnote)
FPG missing rate: 32.95% (GLP-1 RA), 32.66% (insulin), 24.13% (metformin) (Table 3S footnote)

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Outcomes were identified using unvalidated electronic regex text-matching and ICD-10 diagnostic codes across routine electronic health records. Patients on newly adopted, expensive injectable medications (GLP-1 RAs) undergo more intense clinical and laboratory surveillance, inflating diagnostic detection for conditions like acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and cysts.

findings.title: Surveillance and detection bias
findings.mechanism: Patients prescribed GLP-1 RAs had higher socioeconomic status (23.84% vs 21.27% higher education in matched insulin; 75.06% citizen health insurance) and more frequent follow-up testing, increasing incidental detection of subclinical thyroid, renal, and skin conditions.
evidence: Outcomes identified via ICD-10 and regex without medical record adjudication (Table 2S)
Thyroid cancer sHR 2.25 (1.23–4.10) and thyroid dysfunction sHR 1.27 (1.00–1.63) vs metformin (Results 3.2)

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Dozens of disparate exploratory endpoints were tested across multiple GLP-1 RA subclasses and duration cutpoints without adjustment for multiple comparisons, yielding extreme effect sizes for rare outcomes (e.g. leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI 4.65–48.98).

findings.title: Multiplicity and wide exploratory outcome screening
findings.mechanism: Testing over 18 distinct adverse endpoints across multiple drugs and time strata without family-wise error rate control leads to spurious statistical associations.
evidence: Leukemia sHR: 15.09 (95% CI: 4.65–48.98) in GLP-1 RAs ≥12 months vs metformin (Figure 3)
Acne sHR: 5.32 (95% CI: 2.21–12.81) in GLP-1 RAs ≥12 months vs metformin (Figure 3)

overall.summary: The study exhibits a very high risk of bias across multiple domains. Key clinical confounders (diabetes severity, duration, baseline kidney function, and baseline HbA1c which was >90% missing) were uncontrolled, and propensity score matching relied on matching missing categories ('unspecified'). Furthermore, the outcome ascertainment relied on unvalidated EHR regular expression searching vulnerable to surveillance bias, while the inclusion criteria conditioned on long-term monotherapy continuation and treated acute adverse symptoms as competing risks. These methodological limitations, combined with uncontrolled multiple hypothesis testing generating implausibly high hazard ratios across unrelated diseases (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09), severely threaten the validity of the reported conclusions.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Exact incident case counts and event numbers per outcome arm in matched cohorts to compute absolute risk differences and numbers needed to harm.
Complete baseline biochemical data (HbA1c, baseline eGFR, microalbuminuria, lipid profiles) to adjust for confounding by indication without missing indicator categories.
Validated adjudication of ICD-10/regex-identified endpoints to quantify outcome misclassification and diagnostic surveillance bias.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure groups based on treatment patterns evaluated over the entire follow-up period, introducing immortal time bias and conditioning on future exposure. Furthermore, the absence of a lag period combined with a mean follow-up under two years attributes pre-existing indolent malignancies like thyroid cancer to short-term drug exposure.
